{{Short description|Locally connected dendroid}}
In mathematics, a '''dendrite''' is a certain type of [[topological space]] that may be characterized either as a [[locally connected]] [[Dendroid (topology)|dendroid]] or equivalently as a locally connected [[continuum (topology)|continuum]] that contains no simple closed curves.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Whyburn | first = Gordon Thomas | authorlink = Gordon Thomas Whyburn
 | location = New York
 | mr = 0007095
 | page = 88
 | publisher = American Mathematical Society
 | series = American Mathematical Society Colloquium Publications
 | title = Analytic Topology
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=niByQPkPObwC&pg=PA88
 | volume = 28
 | year = 1942}}.</ref>

[[File:Dendrite julia.png|right|thumb|Dendrite Julia set]]

==Importance==
Dendrites may be used to model certain types of [[Julia set]].<ref>{{citation|title=Complex Dynamics|volume=69|series=Universitext|first1=Lennart|last1=Carleson|author1-link=Lennart Carleson|first2=Theodore W.|last2=Gamelin|author-link2=Theodore Gamelin|publisher=Springer|year=1993|isbn=9780387979427|page=94|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M-I8qRE8HGUC&pg=PA94}}.</ref>  For example, if 0 is pre-periodic, but not periodic, under the function <math>f(z) = z^2 + c</math>, then the Julia set of <math>f</math> is a dendrite: connected, without interior.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Devaney | first = Robert L.  | authorlink = Robert L. Devaney
 | mr = 1046376 
 | page = 294
 | publisher = Addison-Wesley Publishing Company
 | series = Studies in Nonlinearity
 | title = An Introduction to Chaotic Dynamical Systems
 | year = 1989}}.</ref>
